title: Easy exam 9
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: if syntax, groups, info, tee, GRUB's command line, mount points, quoting, text tools, ownership and top.

questions.title: An if with several branches
questions.text: Which `if` is written correctly in bash?

options.t: `if [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; then echo pos; elif [ "$n" -lt 0 ]; then echo neg; else echo zero; fi`
options.why: Each test is followed by `;` (or a newline) before `then`, the extra branch is `elif`, and everything ends with `fi`.

options.t: `if [ "$n" -gt 0 ] then echo pos; else if [ "$n" -lt 0 ] then echo neg; fi`
options.why: There is no `;` before `then`, so the shell reports a syntax error near `else`.

options.t: `if [ "$n" -gt 0 ]; then echo pos; elsif [ "$n" -lt 0 ]; then echo neg; fi`
options.why: `elsif` does not exist in bash; the keyword is `elif`.

options.t: `if ["$n" -gt 0]; then echo pos; elif ["$n" -lt 0]; then echo neg; fi`
options.why: `[` is a command and needs spaces around it: `["5"` is read as an unknown command called `[5`.

options.t: Each line has four fields separated by colons: group name, password placeholder, GID and a list of members.
options.why: True: for example `devs:x:1004:luke,sally`.

options.t: The members are written separated by commas.
options.why: True: `luke,sally,rmartin`.

options.t: A user can belong to a group without being named in its member list, if that group is the user's primary group.
options.why: True: the primary group is not taken from this list.

options.t: The primary group of a user is the one that lists the user as a member in `/etc/group`.
options.why: False: the primary group is the GID written in the user's line of `/etc/passwd`; `/etc/group` lists the supplementary members.

options.t: `u` goes up one level of the node tree and `l` goes back to the last node you visited.
options.why: `info` organises a manual as a tree of nodes; `n`, `p`, `u` move through it and `l` goes back.

options.t: `n` and `p` scroll the current node one line down and up.
options.why: They jump to the next and the previous node; scrolling is done with the space bar and backspace.

options.t: `q` goes back to the previous node; to leave `info` you press `x`.
options.why: `q` is the key that quits `info`.

options.t: `Tab` goes to the next page of the node.
options.why: `Tab` moves the cursor to the next link (menu entry or cross-reference) of the node.

questions.title: Screen and file at once
questions.text: Which command shows the output of `ls` on the screen and also saves it in `list.txt`?

options.t: `ls | tee list.txt`
options.why: `tee` copies its input to its output and to the file.

options.t: `ls > list.txt`
options.why: The output goes only to the file; nothing is shown.

options.t: `ls | list.txt`
options.why: The shell tries to run `list.txt` as a command: "command not found".

options.t: `ls | cat > list.txt`
options.why: `cat` just forwards the data, and the `>` sends it to the file: nothing reaches the screen.

questions.title: chainloader in GRUB
questions.text: At the GRUB command line, what is the purpose of `chainloader +1`?

options.t: To hand control to the boot loader of another partition or system, instead of loading a kernel.
options.why: This is chain loading: GRUB does not load a kernel itself but starts the other boot loader.

options.t: To load a Linux kernel into memory and pass it the parameters of the command line.
options.why: That is done with `linux` (and `initrd` for the initial RAM disk).

options.t: To select the partition that holds `/boot`.
options.why: That is done with `set root=...` (or `search`).

options.t: To rebuild `grub.cfg` from the files in `/etc/grub.d/`.
options.why: That is `update-grub`, run from a normal shell, not from the GRUB prompt.

questions.title: A mount point with files
questions.text: The directory `/mnt/data` contains the file `old.txt`. You mount a partition that holds `new.txt` on `/mnt/data`. What does `ls /mnt/data` show?

options.t: Only `new.txt`: `old.txt` is hidden until the partition is unmounted.
options.why: Mounting covers the previous contents of the mount point; they are not deleted and reappear after `umount`.

options.t: Both `old.txt` and `new.txt`, merged in a single listing.
options.why: A mount does not merge directories: it replaces what you see at that path.

options.t: Only `old.txt`, until you `cd` into the directory again.
options.why: The mount takes effect at once for everybody.

options.t: Nothing: the mount point is emptied when something is mounted on it.
options.why: The files are not erased; they are just not reachable while the mount lasts.

options.t: `echo 'Cost: $5 "net"'`
options.why: Single quotes keep every character as it is, double quotes and `$5` included.

options.t: `echo "Cost: $5 "net""`
options.why: Inside double quotes `$5` is expanded (to nothing) and the quotes around `net` just close and reopen the string: it prints `Cost:  net`.

options.t: `echo Cost: $5 "net"`
options.why: `$5` is expanded to nothing and the quotes disappear: it prints `Cost: net`.

options.t: `echo "Cost: $5 \"net\""`
options.why: The `\"` are right, but `$5` is still expanded: it prints `Cost:  "net"`.

options.t: With no options it cuts the input into pieces of 1000 lines.
options.why: True: 1000 lines is the default size.

options.t: `split -b 1M big.bin` cuts the file into pieces of one mebibyte.
options.why: True: `-b` sets the size in bytes (with suffixes such as K and M).

options.t: If no prefix is given, the pieces are called `xaa`, `xab`, `xac`...
options.why: True: the default prefix is `x`.

options.t: `split` deletes the original file after cutting it.
options.why: False: `split` only reads the file; the original is still there afterwards.

questions.title: Who can change the owner
questions.text: Which statement about `chown` and `chgrp` is TRUE?

options.t: Only root can give a file away; the owner can change its group, but only to a group he or she is in.
options.why: As an ordinary user, `chown root file` fails with "Operation not permitted", and so does `chgrp` with a group you are not in.

options.t: The owner of a file can give it to any other existing user of the system with `chown`.
options.why: Allowing that would let users dodge disk quotas, so Linux restricts it to root.

options.t: `chgrp` changes the permission bits of the group on a file.
options.why: `chgrp` changes which group owns the file; the bits are changed with `chmod`.

options.t: `chown` can only be used on directories.
options.why: It works on any file.

questions.title: Sorting inside top
questions.text: While `top` is running you press `M` (capital). What happens?

options.t: The list is sorted by memory usage.
options.why: Inside `top`, `M` sorts by `%MEM`; `P` sorts by CPU usage.

options.t: The list is sorted by CPU usage.
options.why: That is the key `P`.

options.t: A prompt asks for the PID of a process to kill.
options.why: That is `k`.

options.t: `top` quits.
options.why: That is `q`.
